chapters.title: Chapter 1: Thinking Like a Hedger, Not a Trader

lessons.title: Moneyness and Strike Choice Through an Insurance Lens

children.text: When you buy health insurance, the premium changes with the deductible. Agree to pay the first ₹50,000 of every claim yourself and your premium drops sharply. Insist on the insurer paying from the very first rupee and it goes up. Put options work the same way, and the strike price is your deductible. Open the Nifty option chain and you will see a dozen or more strikes for every expiry. Most investors pick whichever looks cheap. A hedger picks the strike that caps the loss at a level they can actually live with, and no lower than that. This lesson shows you how.

body.text: The strike price of a put is the deductible on your insurance. The lower the strike, the cheaper the cover and the more of the fall you absorb yourself. Choose the strike from your tolerable drawdown, never from the price tag.

children.text: Moneyness: Where the Strike Sits Against Today's Price

markDefs.definition: Where an option's strike sits relative to the current price of the underlying, which decides whether the option has intrinsic value today.

children.text: describes whether an option would have any value if it expired right now. There are three labels, and they flip between calls and puts, because a call wants the price above the strike and a put wants it below.

cells: Strike at or nearest current price
Strike at or nearest current price

body.title: Locate the OTM put
body.textWithBlank: An out-of-the-money put has a strike price ___ the current price of the underlying.
body.explanation: A put only has intrinsic value when the price is below the strike. If the strike is already below today's price, the market has to fall to that strike before the put starts paying out, so it is out of the money.

children.text: Reading Moneyness as an Insurance Policy
For a hedger holding a Nifty-like portfolio, each moneyness label maps neatly to a type of insurance policy.

body.caption: Put moneyness translated into insurance language

cells: A policy that pays out on a claim that has, in effect, already happened
Mostly intrinsic value you pay for in full upfront. Expensive, and most of the premium is not insurance at all
Cover from the first rupee of loss. The most expensive pure insurance
You absorb small falls and are protected from meaningful ones. The usual hedger's zone
Very cheap, but only pays in a crash. Your portfolio takes the full hit of any ordinary correction

children.text: Now put real numbers on it. Here are three-month Nifty puts across strikes, with the Nifty at 25,000 and one lot of 65 units protecting ₹16,25,000 of exposure.

body.caption: S = Nifty today, K = put strike, P = put premium. The first term is your deductible, the second is the cost of cover.
Three-month Nifty puts, Nifty at 25,000, one lot of 65 (illustrative premiums)
headers: Rough yearly cost if rolled every quarter

body.title: The strike trade-off: cheaper cover means a bigger worst case

body.text: Look at the ITM row. The 25,500 put costs ₹680, but ₹500 of that is intrinsic value you are simply prepaying. Only ₹180 is actual insurance. A hedger almost never needs ITM puts. And notice how fast costs climb as you move towards the money: the 25,000 put costs nearly ten times the 22,000 put. The first few percent of protection are by far the most expensive.

body.title: Calculate the worst case
body.prompt: The Nifty is at 25,000. You hedge a Nifty-tracking portfolio with the 24,500 put at ₹340. What is your maximum hedged loss, as a percentage of the portfolio? (Two decimal places.)
body.explanation: Deductible: (25,000 − 24,500) ÷ 25,000 = 2.00%. Cost of cover: 340 ÷ 25,000 = 1.36%. Maximum hedged loss = 2.00% + 1.36% = 3.36%. Tight protection, but at 1.36% for three months, it would cost over 5% a year to keep rolling.

children.text: From Tolerable Drawdown to Strike: A Worked Example

In Lesson 2 you learned to calculate a tolerable drawdown. Here is where it pays off. The rule is simple: pick the lowest-cost strike whose maximum hedged loss stays within your tolerable drawdown, with a buffer for the fact that your portfolio will not track the Nifty perfectly.

Harish, 55, is a textile exporter in Tiruppur. He holds ₹32,50,000 in a Nifty 50 index fund, which is exactly two Nifty lots at 25,000 (2 × 65 × 25,000). The final ₹30 lakh payment on his new flat is due in three months, and the builder will not wait. His tolerable drawdown is 1 − 30 ÷ 32.5 = 7.69%.

body.caption: Harish's candidate strikes: two lots (130 units), portfolio ₹32,50,000, needs ₹30,00,000

children.text: The 23,000 put is cheapest but fails the test. The 23,500 put is the cheapest that passes, but a buffer of ₹33,550, about 1% of the portfolio, is thin. His index fund has a small tracking difference, and any costs of redeeming come out of the same pot. The 24,000 put costs ₹11,050 more and nearly triples the buffer. The 24,500 put adds very little extra safety for a lot more premium. For Harish, 24,000 is the sensible choice: comfortably within his limit, without paying for protection he does not need.

body.title: Harish's worst case with the 24,000 put: ₹1,62,500

body.text: This clean result depends on Harish owning a Nifty 50 index fund. If he held midcap or sectoral funds instead, his portfolio could fall well more than the Nifty, and a Nifty put would not cover the difference. In that case he would need a bigger buffer or a different approach. Chapter 3 deals with exactly this problem.

columns.label: Near the money (0% to 4% below)
points: Starts paying out after a small fall
Expensive: 1% to 2% of the portfolio per quarter
Suits a hard, near-term goal with a small tolerable drawdown

columns.label: Far out of the money (10% or more below)
points: Pays only in a genuine crash
You absorb every ordinary correction yourself
Cheap: a fraction of a percent per quarter
Suits long-term investors guarding against catastrophe only
Easy to overbuy because each lot looks inexpensive

body.title: Match the strike to the investor
body.question: Rukmini, 40, has ₹16 lakh in a Nifty 50 index fund and no goals due for 15 years. She is not worried about ordinary 10% corrections, but wants some protection against a 2008-style collapse while spending as little as possible. With the Nifty at 25,000, which three-month put fits best?
body.explanation: Rukmini wants catastrophe-only cover at minimal cost, and her long horizon means she can absorb ordinary corrections. The far OTM 22,000 put costs about 0.2% per quarter and caps her loss at roughly 12% over the period. The ATM and ITM puts are expensive protection against falls she has said she can live with.

body.title: The ₹5 put habit
body.scenario: Arjun, 31, works in sales in Gurugram and has ₹16 lakh in Nifty index funds. Every week he buys one lot of a Nifty put about 12% below the current level, expiring that same week, for around ₹5. "It's only ₹325 a week," he says. "If there's ever a crash, I'm covered."
body.prompt: Is Arjun's approach a sensible hedge? Think about the deductible, how often it could pay out, and the total cost.
body.modelAnswer:
1. The deductible is huge for the time covered. A 12% fall inside a single week is extremely rare for the Nifty and has happened only in extreme crises. Most crashes, including the worst of 2008, unfolded over weeks or months, so a weekly 12% OTM put would usually expire worthless even during a severe bear market.
2. The cost adds up. ₹325 a week over 52 weeks is ₹16,900 a year, about 1% of his portfolio, for cover that almost never pays.
3. For roughly the same yearly spend, a three-month 22,000 put rolled each quarter (about ₹3,250 per quarter, ₹13,000 a year) gives similar catastrophe protection that stays in place for a whole quarter, so it can actually catch a slow-motion crash.
4. Even better for a 31-year-old with a long horizon and an SIP: ask whether he needs to pay for crash protection at all.
The lesson: a strike is only meaningful alongside its expiry. A cheap premium on cover that can almost never pay out is not cheap.

children.text: The same insurance thinking applies when you sell covered calls in Chapter 4, just in reverse. Selling an OTM call means agreeing to give up any gains above that strike in exchange for premium. A call far above the current price brings in very little premium but rarely caps your upside. A call close to the current price pays more but will often cost you a rally. Investors who want to keep their shares usually sell OTM calls, for the same reason hedgers usually buy OTM puts: a sensible balance between cost and what you give up.

body.title: Choose a strike the hedger's way
steps: Calculate your tolerable drawdown: 1 minus the amount needed divided by the portfolio value.
Open the option chain for an expiry that covers your full risk period, not just this week.
For four or five put strikes below the current level, calculate the deductible, the cost of cover and the maximum hedged loss.
Eliminate any strike whose maximum hedged loss exceeds your tolerable drawdown.
From the remaining strikes, pick the cheapest one that still leaves a buffer of at least 1% to 2%, more if your portfolio does not closely track the index.

cards.definition: Strike above the current price. The put already has intrinsic value.
Strike at or nearest to the current price. Highest time value.
Strike below the current price. No intrinsic value, only time value.
For a protective put, the fall from today's price to the strike, which you absorb yourself: (S − K) ÷ S.
Deductible plus cost of cover: (S − K) ÷ S + P ÷ S.
A far OTM put that is cheap but only pays out in a severe crash.

points: Moneyness compares strike and current price. A put is ITM above the current price, ATM at it, and OTM below it.
For a hedger, the put strike is the deductible: lower strikes mean cheaper cover but a larger share of the fall is yours.
Maximum hedged loss = (S − K) ÷ S + P ÷ S. Calculate it for every strike you consider.
Choose the cheapest strike whose maximum hedged loss sits within your tolerable drawdown, with a buffer for tracking differences.
ITM puts are mostly prepaid intrinsic value, and ATM puts are very costly to hold year-round. Most hedgers live in the OTM zone.
Always judge a strike together with its expiry. Cheap cover that can almost never pay out is not cheap.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Option premiums and the yearly cost estimates are illustrative, and real premiums change with volatility and time. Examples assume the portfolio moves exactly with the Nifty 50, which real portfolios do not. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before using options.
